entries.question: Did a fish or a whale swallow Jonah?
entries.summary: Jonah 1:17 (Hebrew 2:1) says YHWH appointed a dag gadol — a great fish — to swallow Jonah. Matthew 12:40 has Jesus refer to the same incident, but the Greek word used is kētos, traditionally rendered 'whale' in English versions following the KJV. The contradiction is partly a translation artifact (kētos is broader than the modern 'whale') but reflects a genuine LXX-to-NT terminological shift.
entries.commentary:
Start with the Hebrew. Jonah 1:17 (numbered Jonah 2:1 in the MT) reads vayman YHWH dag gadol livloa et-yonah — YHWH appointed a great fish to swallow Jonah. The word dag is the generic Hebrew word for fish, with no taxonomic precision. Jack Sasson in the AB Jonah notes that the Hebrew imagination didn't distinguish whales from large fish — cetaceans were just big fish — so dag gadol covers everything from a large tuna to a whale to a mythological sea-monster. The Hebrew is precise about size (gadol) and vague about species.

The Greek translators of the LXX rendered dag gadol as kētei megalō. The word kētos in Greek covers everything from large fish to whales to mythological sea-monsters — it's the word used for the sea-creatures in Homer and for the Greek Andromeda-rescue mythology. Aristotle uses kētos broadly. So kētos is etymologically and lexically the right Greek word for an unspecified large sea-creature. Matthew 12:40, when Jesus refers to the Jonah incident, picks up the LXX vocabulary directly: en tē koilia tou kētous — in the belly of the kētos.

The KJV translates kētos as 'whale.' That's a 1611 English translation choice based on the dominant Renaissance understanding of kētos as 'whale,' but it's not what kētos means lexically. Modern critical translations are split: the NRSV and NASB render Matthew 12:40 as 'sea monster,' the ESV and NIV as 'great fish' or 'huge fish,' while the NABRE retains the traditional 'whale.' Davies and Allison in the ICC Matthew acknowledge that the KJV rendering as 'whale' is misleading but note that the underlying Greek does not specify whale.

So the contradiction in its strong form — 'fish vs. whale' — dissolves into a translation issue. The KJV created the whale-vs-fish puzzle through anachronistic translation choices, and modern critical translations would render both passages with parallel vocabulary (large fish / sea-creature). The underlying Greek is not asserting whale-specifically.

But don't let the apologist celebrate too early. The harmonization saves Matthew 12:40 from a fish-vs-whale contradiction with Jonah 1:17 at the cost of conceding that the KJV — the translation that for four centuries shaped Anglophone Christian understanding of the text — was wrong about what Matthew said. And the deeper problem with Matthew 12:40 isn't the fish-vs-whale dispute; it's that the verse predicts Jesus will be 'three days and three nights' in the heart of the earth, while the Synoptic crucifixion-resurrection chronology has him buried Friday evening and rising Sunday morning — at most two nights and one full day. Dale Allison in *Resurrecting Jesus* documents this as one of the more genuinely difficult Synoptic chronology problems, and it's a problem this SAB entry doesn't even raise. The fish-vs-whale framing is mostly a KJV-translation artifact. The three-days-and-three-nights problem is real and unresolved.

entries.question: Who cast Jonah into the sea?
entries.summary: Jonah 1:15 says the sailors picked Jonah up and hurled him into the sea. Jonah 2:3, in the prayer from the fish's belly, says God cast him into the deep. So the same narrative, separated by a single chapter, attributes the throwing to two different agents.
entries.commentary:
Look, the surface reading is straightforward. Chapter 1 verse 15 is a third-person narrative report — the sailors take Jonah and throw him in (Hebrew *wayyiśʾû ʾet-yônâ wayĕṭiluhû ʾel-hayyām*). Chapter 2 verse 3 is Jonah's own voice in the psalm of thanksgiving, addressing YHWH directly: *wattašlîkēnî mĕṣûlâ* — 'and you cast me into the deep.' Two different subjects of the verb, same event.

The apologist playbook here is the standard 'dual causation' move — Archer, Geisler, and most evangelical commentators argue that the sailors were the proximate cause and God was the ultimate cause, so both statements are true at different levels. Fair enough as theology. But it's a post-hoc rationalization of a narrative tension the text itself doesn't resolve. Jonah's prayer is structured as a psalm of individual lament (cf. Sasson, *Jonah* AB 24B), and the language of God 'casting' the supplicant into the depths is conventional psalmic imagery (Ps 88:6-7), not a careful theological claim about secondary causation.

The more parsimonious reading is what critical scholars like Limburg and Trible have been saying for decades: the prayer in chapter 2 is a literary insertion — likely a pre-existing psalm appropriated by the author — and it doesn't track the narrative details of chapter 1 with precision. That's why Jonah ends up praying from inside the fish about being cast into the sea by God when the narrative just told us the sailors did it under duress. The prayer was retrofit; the seams show.

Verdict: the literal reading produces two different agents. The harmonization works only if you assume the narrator and the psalmist were coordinating their language with a doctrine of primary/secondary causation neither text actually invokes.

entries.question: Does the Bible condemn astrology?
entries.summary: Leviticus 19:26 and Deuteronomy 18:10-12 ban divination and observing 'times' — language traditionally read to include astrology — and call practitioners an abomination. Genesis 1:14 says God explicitly made the heavenly lights to function as signs. The two passages pull in opposite directions on whether reading the sky is forbidden practice or divinely sanctioned function.
entries.commentary:
The Hebrew here matters. Leviticus 19:26 forbids *meʿônēn* (a Poel participle from a root often glossed 'observer of times' or 'soothsayer'). Deuteronomy 18:10-12 repeats *meʿônēn* in a list with *qôsēm* (diviner) and *mĕnaḥēš* (augur). Whatever the exact technique, this is the priestly polemic against extra-cultic prognostication, and astrology fits the semantic field (cf. Milgrom, *Leviticus 17-22* AB 3A).

Genesis 1:14, by contrast, says the luminaries are *lĕʾōtōt ûlmôʿădîm* — 'for signs and for seasons.' The word *ʾōt* is the same word used in Isaiah 7 for the sign of Immanuel and in Genesis 9 for the rainbow. P (the Priestly source — scholars call the Pentateuchal sources J, E, D, and P) is clearly framing the heavenly bodies as semiotic instruments. That is exactly what astrology claims they are.

The standard apologist harmonization, run by Archer and the IVP *Hard Sayings* crew, is that *ʾōt* in Genesis 1:14 means liturgical calendar markers (festival dates, agricultural seasons) — not predictive omens. That reading isn't crazy. *Môʿădîm* clearly does mean appointed festival times. But limiting *ʾōt* to calendar function ignores how the same author uses *ʾōt* throughout P and how ancient Near Eastern audiences actually read celestial signs. Mesopotamian astral omen literature (*Enuma Anu Enlil*) is exactly the cultural matrix Genesis 1 is written in conversation with — and the polemic is about *who* controls the signs (YHWH, not Marduk), not whether signs exist.

So the tension is real but qualified. Genesis 1 endorses celestial signs as a category; Leviticus and Deuteronomy criminalize the practitioners who read them. The harmonization that says 'signs but only calendar signs' is a post-hoc narrowing. The Bible's own subsequent narrative — Matthew's magi following a star to Bethlehem — shows the tradition itself couldn't keep that line clean.

entries.question: On what did Jesus ride into Jerusalem?
entries.summary: Matthew 21:5-7 has Jesus ride into Jerusalem on two animals — a donkey and a colt — with the disciples laying garments on both and Jesus sitting on 'them.' Mark 11:7 and Luke 19:35 have him ride a single colt. John 12:14 has him on a 'young donkey.' Matthew's two-animal version is unique among the four gospels.
entries.commentary:
Here's the thing — this is one of the cleanest examples of Matthew clumsily literalizing an Old Testament prophecy. Zechariah 9:9 reads (NRSV): 'humble and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey.' That's standard Hebrew synonymous parallelism — one animal, described twice for poetic emphasis (cf. Meyers and Meyers, *Zechariah 9-14* AB 25C). Mark, Luke, and John all read it that way: one animal.

Matthew didn't. Matthew 21:7 says they brought *tēn onon kai ton pōlon* ('the donkey and the colt'), put garments *ep' autōn* ('on them'), and Jesus sat *epanō autōn* ('upon them'). Whether Matthew imagined Jesus straddling both animals at once or shifting between them is a problem the text creates and doesn't solve.

The apologist harmonization, defended by Blomberg in *The Historical Reliability of the Gospels* and by Carson in the Expositor's commentary, runs two ways. Path one: 'them' refers to the garments, not the animals. That's syntactically possible but awkward — the immediate antecedent is the animals, not the garments. Path two: the mother donkey was led alongside and Jesus actually rode the colt; Matthew just got vague. That requires reading Mark/Luke/John back into Matthew, which is exactly the maneuver historical critics object to.

The consensus reading among critical scholars — Davies and Allison's three-volume ICC, Luz's Hermeneia, Nolland's NIGTC — is that Matthew misread the Hebrew parallelism, took 'a donkey and a colt' as two animals, and adjusted his Markan source to fit. It's not a contradiction in the sense that the same event is described two incompatible ways; it's a contradiction in the sense that Matthew's version has Jesus doing something physically awkward to satisfy a prophecy that didn't require it.

Verdict: Mark/Luke/John have one animal. Matthew has two. The harmonization either tortures the syntax or admits Matthew was vague in a way that conveniently looks like Mark/Luke/John.

entries.question: Can God be tempted?
entries.books_in_tension: Exodus, Deuteronomy, Malachi, Judith, Matthew, Luke, Acts, Hebrews, James
entries.summary: James 1:13 says God cannot be tempted with evil (*apeirastos kakōn*). But Deuteronomy 6:16, Exodus 17:2, Matthew 4:7, Luke 4:12, and Acts 15:10 all assume God can be tempted — the command 'do not tempt God' presupposes the act is possible. And Hebrews 4:15 says Jesus, identified as God by orthodox Christology, was tempted in every way.
entries.commentary:
James 1:13 is unambiguous in the Greek: *ho gar theos apeirastos estin kakōn* — 'for God is untemptable with respect to evils.' The adjective *apeirastos* is rare (a *hapax legomenon* in the New Testament) and the construction is categorical. God can't be tempted. Full stop.

Meanwhile the Old and New Testaments are saturated with the assumption that God *can* be tempted — that's why the Torah has to forbid it. Deuteronomy 6:16, *lōʾ tĕnassû ʾet-YHWH ʾĕlōhêkem* — 'you shall not test YHWH your God.' Exodus 17:2 uses the same root *nsh* when Moses accuses Israel of testing God at Massah. Jesus quotes Deuteronomy 6:16 back at Satan in Matthew 4:7 and Luke 4:12. Peter uses *peirazete* in Acts 15:10. The whole biblical vocabulary of 'testing/tempting God' uses the same Hebrew root *nsh* and Greek root *peirazō* that James says is impossible.

The apologist harmonization — Moo in the Pillar volume and Davids in the NIGTC on James — is that James means God cannot be tempted *toward* evil (i.e., God cannot be enticed to sin), whereas the testing passages mean humans cannot legitimately put God on trial. Two different senses of *peirazō*. That distinction is real in Greek lexicography (BDAG entry on *peirazō* gives both 'test' and 'tempt to sin'). Fair.

But here's the problem: Hebrews 4:15 explicitly says Jesus was *pepeirasmenon de kata panta kath' homoiotēta* — 'tempted in every respect, like we are.' Same verb, *peirazō*. If Jesus is God (entry 400 in this very database), and Jesus was tempted *kata panta* (in every way) like us, then the *apeirastos kakōn* of James 1:13 is in direct tension with the Chalcedonian Christology Hebrews assumes.

The scholarly consensus (Allison's ICC on James, Johnson's AB) is that James 1:13 reflects a Hellenistic Jewish theological commitment (God's impassibility) that doesn't fully cohere with the rest of the canon's narrative theology. It's the kind of contradiction that emerges when philosophically tidy claims meet narrative texts. Take your pick: either James is using *apeirastos* in a restricted technical sense the rest of the canon doesn't honor, or the canon itself is incoherent on whether God is temptable.

entries.question: From which of David's sons was Jesus descended?
entries.summary: Matthew 1:6-16 traces Jesus's lineage through David's son Solomon. Luke 3:23-31 traces it through David's son Nathan. Both genealogies claim to give Joseph's ancestry, but they pass through two different sons of David and produce two almost entirely different lists of names between David and Joseph.
entries.commentary:
This is the genealogy problem that has tortured harmonizers for nineteen centuries. Matthew 1 runs David → Solomon → Rehoboam (Matthew's 'Roboam') → the kings of Judah → Joseph. Luke 3 runs David → Nathan → an entirely different sequence of unknown names → Joseph. They share David and they share Joseph and almost nothing in between.

The two main harmonizations both have problems.

Harmonization one — going back to Africanus in the third century and revived by Machen — is the levirate-marriage theory: one genealogy gives Joseph's biological father, the other gives his legal father under levirate law (Deut 25:5-10). That requires postulating a specific levirate marriage at exactly the generation needed to make the lines diverge and reconverge, with no textual support anywhere in the New Testament. It's the textbook *ad hoc* fix.

Harmonization two — popularized by John Lightfoot and still used by modern apologists like Geisler — is that Matthew gives Joseph's lineage and Luke gives Mary's. The problem is that Luke 3:23 explicitly says *hōs enomizeto huios Iōsēph tou Hēli* — 'being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph, the son of Heli.' Luke is naming Joseph's ancestry, not Mary's. To make Luke be about Mary you have to read 'son of Heli' as 'son-in-law of Heli,' which the Greek does not naturally support and which no first-century reader would have inferred.

The critical consensus — Brown in *Birth of the Messiah*, Fitzmyer in the AB Luke, Bauckham in *Jude and the Relatives of Jesus* — is that the two genealogies are independent theological constructions, both designed to establish Davidic descent but drawing on different source traditions and serving different theological aims. Matthew's royal-Solomonic line emphasizes Jesus as kingly messiah; Luke's Nathan line may reflect a tradition that linked the messiah to the priestly/prophetic Nathan rather than the failed Judahite kings (cf. Zech 12:12 which singles out 'the house of Nathan' in messianic mourning).

Verdict: the two genealogies cannot both be Joseph's biological ancestry. The harmonizations require either inventing a levirate marriage with no evidence or forcing Luke's Greek to mean what it doesn't say. Take your pick.

entries.question: Who was Jesus's paternal grandfather?
entries.summary: Matthew 1:16 names Jacob as the father of Joseph and therefore Jesus's paternal grandfather. Luke 3:23 names Heli as the father of Joseph. The two genealogies disagree on the most recent ancestor of Joseph, not just the distant ancestry.
entries.commentary:
This is the same problem as entry 386 narrowed to a single generation. Matthew 1:16 — *Iakōb de egennēsen ton Iōsēph ton andra Marias* (Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary). Luke 3:23 — *Iōsēph tou Hēli* (Joseph of Heli, i.e., son of Heli). One says Joseph's father was Jacob. The other says it was Heli.

The apologist responses are the same as the larger genealogy contradiction. The levirate-marriage harmonization (Africanus, Machen) says Heli died childless, his brother Jacob married the widow, fathered Joseph who was therefore Heli's legal son and Jacob's biological son. Possible in the abstract but unsupported by any independent evidence — and notice that to make this work for *just* this generation, the harmonizer has to also explain why the entire genealogies above this point diverge, which the levirate fix doesn't address.

The Mary's-genealogy harmonization (Lightfoot, Geisler, the IVP commentaries) says Heli was Mary's father, and Luke 3:23 should be read as 'Joseph, son-in-law of Heli.' The Greek doesn't support this — *tou Hēli* is the same genitive construction Luke uses for every other father-son link in the genealogy, and there's no precedent in ancient Greek genealogies for a son-in-law slot being silently substituted.

The parsimonious critical reading is that Matthew and Luke drew on different traditional materials, both of which independently claimed to give Joseph's ancestry, and the redactors made no attempt to reconcile them. The two infancy narratives don't agree on much else either — Matthew has magi and a flight to Egypt; Luke has shepherds and an early return to Nazareth. The genealogies are part of a larger pattern of independent traditions about Jesus's origins that fit awkwardly together (cf. Brown, *Birth of the Messiah*).

Verdict: Matthew says Jacob. Luke says Heli. The harmonizations require inventing a levirate marriage or grammatically forcing 'son-in-law' into Greek that doesn't say it. Neither is parsimonious.

entries.question: How many generations from Jesus to Abraham?
entries.summary: Matthew 1:17 states explicitly: 14 generations from Abraham to David, 14 from David to the deportation, 14 from the deportation to Christ — 42 total. Count the actual names in Matthew 1:1-17 and you get 41. Matthew's stated arithmetic does not match Matthew's own list.
entries.commentary:
This is one of the cleanest internal contradictions in the New Testament because it's Matthew vs. Matthew. The author asserts a numerical scheme (3 x 14 = 42) and then provides the list that doesn't add up.

Count the names: Abraham to David inclusive is 14 (Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Judah, Perez, Hezron, Ram, Amminadab, Nahshon, Salmon, Boaz, Obed, Jesse, David). David to the deportation (Jeconiah) is 14 *if* you count David twice (David, Solomon, Rehoboam, Abijah, Asa, Jehoshaphat, Joram, Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, Hezekiah, Manasseh, Amon, Josiah, Jeconiah — that's 15 starting from David, or 14 starting from Solomon). The deportation to Christ is only 13 (Jeconiah, Shealtiel, Zerubbabel, Abiud, Eliakim, Azor, Zadok, Achim, Eliud, Eleazar, Matthan, Jacob, Joseph, Jesus — that's 14 if you count Jeconiah twice, or 13 if you don't).

The apologist harmonization, run by Carson in EBC and the standard evangelical introductions, is that David and Jeconiah are pivot figures counted in both their adjacent groups, which lets you get 14 + 14 + 14 with the same person doing double duty. That works mathematically but it's a manipulation — you're claiming 42 generations while only having 41 distinct individuals. If David and Jeconiah each count twice, the *generation count* from Abraham to Jesus is 41, not 42, because a person isn't two generations.

The critical consensus (Davies-Allison ICC, Luz Hermeneia, Brown *Birth of the Messiah*) is that Matthew himself knew the numbers were tight — the 3x14 scheme is built on the gematria of David's name (D-V-D = 4+6+4 = 14) — and he made the count work by manipulating his source. He may have dropped three Judahite kings (Ahaziah, Joash, Amaziah between Joram and Uzziah, cf. 1 Chr 3:11-12) precisely to hit his 14-14-14 target. The arithmetic problem is what's left over after the manipulation.

Verdict: Matthew claims 42, Matthew lists 41. The harmonization that counts David and Jeconiah twice produces 42 generation-slots but only 41 generations of human beings. The numerology is doing the work; the genealogy is paying the cost.

entries.question: How many generations were between the Babylonian captivity and Jesus?
entries.summary: Matthew 1:17 states there are 14 generations from the deportation to Babylon to Christ. Matthew 1:12-16 actually lists Jechonias, Shealtiel, Zerubbabel, Abiud, Eliakim, Azor, Zadok, Achim, Eliud, Eleazar, Matthan, Jacob, Joseph, Jesus — that's 13 begettings if Jechonias is the last pre-exilic figure, or 13 distinct individuals after Jechonias. Matthew's stated count of 14 does not match Matthew's own list of begettings for the third section.
entries.commentary:
This is the same arithmetic problem as entry 388, isolated to the third panel. Matthew 1:17 says 14 generations from the deportation to Christ. The list in 1:12-16, counted as begettings (the explicit *egennēsen* clauses), gives you only 13.

Matthew 1:12 — Jechonias begat Salathiel (1). Salathiel begat Zorobabel (2). Zorobabel begat Abiud (3). Abiud begat Eliakim (4). Eliakim begat Azor (5). Azor begat Sadoc (6). Sadoc begat Achim (7). Achim begat Eliud (8). Eliud begat Eleazar (9). Eleazar begat Matthan (10). Matthan begat Jacob (11). Jacob begat Joseph (12). And then Joseph is the husband of Mary 'of whom was born Jesus' — Jesus (13). That's 13 *egennēsen*-style transitions, or 13 generations after Jechonias, depending on how you count Jesus.

The apologist harmonization — Carson, Blomberg, the *Hard Sayings* commentary — counts Jechonias as the first of the third group (he was deported, so he straddles), which gives you Jechonias (1), Salathiel (2), ... Jesus (14). That works numerically. But it requires Jechonias to count both as the endpoint of group two ('from David to the deportation are fourteen generations,' which lands on Jechonias) and as the startpoint of group three. He's the double-counted pivot.

The critical reading (Davies-Allison, Luz, Brown) is that the third panel is genuinely short — only 13 generations — and the author either (a) miscounted, (b) is using 'fourteen' loosely, or (c) intended us to count Jesus and Christ as two events ('born' Jesus + becoming 'Christ' at baptism/resurrection). Option (c) is the desperate fix; options (a) and (b) admit the obvious.

The deeper issue is that the third panel covers roughly 600 years (from ca. 597 BCE deportation to ca. 4 BCE birth) and lists only 13-14 names, which gives you ~46 years per generation. The first panel (Abraham to David) covers roughly a millennium and lists 14 names — ~71 years per generation. The middle panel covers ~400 years with 14 names — ~29 years per generation. The math is incoherent across the panels because the genealogy isn't trying to be historical; it's trying to be theological-numerological. The Davidic gematria (D-V-D = 14) is the organizing principle, and where the source data didn't fit the scheme, Matthew dropped names or fudged counts.

Verdict: Matthew says 14 in the third panel. Matthew lists 13 begettings. The harmonization makes Jechonias count twice. Take your pick.

entries.question: Was Joseph the father of Jesus?
entries.books_in_tension: Matthew, Luke, Acts, Romans, 2 Timothy, Hebrews, Revelation
entries.summary: Acts 2:30, Acts 13:23, Romans 1:3, 2 Timothy 2:8, Hebrews 2:16, and Revelation 22:16 all describe Jesus as physically descended from David 'according to the flesh.' Davidic descent in this canon runs exclusively through Joseph (Matt 1:6-16; Luke 3:23-31 both trace it through him). But Matthew 1:18-25 and Luke 1:31-35 say Mary conceived by the Holy Spirit and Joseph was not the biological father. If Joseph wasn't the father, the Davidic descent claim has no biological mechanism.
entries.commentary:
This is the contradiction that virgin-birth Christology built into itself the moment it landed in a canon that also insists on Davidic descent *kata sarka*.

Paul says it plainly in Romans 1:3 — Jesus *tou genomenou ek spermatos Dauid kata sarka* (born of the seed of David according to the flesh). The phrase *kata sarka* (according to the flesh) is not metaphorical here — Paul contrasts it with *kata pneuma hagiōsynēs* (according to the spirit of holiness) in the next verse. The fleshly mechanism is genealogical inheritance through male line. That was how 'seed of David' worked in Second Temple messianism (cf. 4QFlor; *Psalms of Solomon* 17).

Matthew and Luke both give genealogies that run through Joseph (not Mary) precisely because that's how Davidic descent is established. Then Matthew 1:18 says *eurethē en gastri echousa ek pneumatos hagiou* — 'she was found with child of the Holy Spirit' — and Luke 1:35 has the angel say *pneuma hagion epeleusetai epi se* — 'the Holy Spirit will come upon you.' Joseph is removed from the biological chain. So either the Davidic-descent claim collapses, or Joseph is the biological father after all.

The standard apologist harmonization is adoption: Jesus was Joseph's *legal* son under Jewish law, and legal sonship transmits inheritance rights including the Davidic claim. Brown discusses this carefully in *Birth of the Messiah* (pp. 138-139). It works for inheritance — Joseph naming the child (Matt 1:25, Luke 2:21) is the formal act of paternal acknowledgment. But it doesn't work for *kata sarka*. Paul, the author of Acts, the author of Hebrews, and John of Patmos are not making a legal-inheritance claim — they're making a fleshly-descent claim. 'Seed of David according to the flesh' is biology, not adoption law.

An alternative harmonization (the one developed in late antiquity and codified in Justin and Irenaeus) is that Mary herself was secretly of Davidic descent, transmitting the Davidic gene through her. But neither Matthew nor Luke says this — they give Joseph's genealogy, not Mary's. The Mary-Davidic-descent claim is a post-canonical patch.

Verdict: the canon claims both that Jesus is Joseph's biological flesh-descendant of David and that Joseph is not Jesus's biological father. Pick one.

entries.question: When was Jesus born?
entries.summary: Matthew 2:1 places Jesus's birth 'in the days of Herod the king' — meaning before Herod the Great's death in 4 BCE. Luke 1:5 likewise puts the conception under Herod, but Luke 2:1-4 anchors the birth to the census 'when Quirinius was governor of Syria.' Quirinius's documented census was 6 CE, after Judaea became a Roman province. The two anchor points are about a decade apart and cannot both be correct.
entries.commentary:
This is one of the best-documented chronological problems in the New Testament. The two dating anchors are independently verifiable from non-biblical sources, and they don't fit.

Matthew 2 places the birth before Herod's death. Herod died in 4 BCE — Josephus, *Antiquities* 17.167-191 and 17.213, dates it precisely, and the date is confirmed by the lunar eclipse that preceded his death. Matthew's narrative requires this — the magi visit Herod, Herod orders the Bethlehem massacre, the family flees to Egypt and only returns after Herod is dead (Matt 2:19-20). The terminus ante quem is 4 BCE.

Luke 2:2 says *hautē apographē prōtē egeneto hēgemoneuontos tēs Syrias Kyrēniou* — 'this was the first census while Quirinius was governing Syria.' Publius Sulpicius Quirinius's governorship and the associated census are dated by Josephus (*Antiquities* 18.1-2) to 6 CE, when Judaea was first absorbed as a Roman province after the deposition of Archelaus. That's the census that triggered the revolt of Judas the Galilean (Acts 5:37 alludes to the same event).

The gap between Herod's death and the Quirinius census is at least 9-10 years.

The apologist harmonizations have been industrial. The two most common: (1) translate *prōtē* not as 'first' but as 'before' (i.e., 'this census was before the one when Quirinius governed Syria'), and (2) postulate an earlier, undocumented Quirinius governorship. Both fail. The 'before' reading was floated by N. T. Wright but is grammatically strained — *prōtē* with a genitive absolute is a superlative, not a comparative, and the natural reading is 'first.' The earlier-Quirinius theory was destroyed by Sherwin-White and confirmed dead by every Roman historian who's looked at it — there's no archaeological or literary evidence for Quirinius governing Syria before 6 CE, and the gap is filled by other named legates (Sentius Saturninus, Quinctilius Varus, Volusius Saturninus). The *Lapis Tiburtinus* inscription sometimes cited for an earlier Quirinius posting doesn't actually name him and doesn't refer to Syria.

The critical consensus (Brown, Fitzmyer, Bovon, Carrier, even some moderate evangelicals like Ben Witherington) is that Luke conflated the 6 CE census of Judaea with the birth of Jesus (which actually occurred under Herod) because he needed a Roman administrative event to motivate the Bethlehem trip from Nazareth — that's the device that gets a Galilean couple to David's hometown.

Verdict: Matthew's date is before 4 BCE. Luke's census-date is 6 CE. The two cannot both be right. The harmonizations require either inventing an undocumented earlier Quirinius governorship or torturing the Greek. Take your pick.

entries.question: Was Jesus born in a house or a manger?
entries.summary: Luke 2:1-7 has Mary deliver Jesus and lay him in a manger because there was no room at the inn. Matthew 2:1-2, 11 has the magi visit the family in a house. The two birth narratives place the infant Jesus in two different physical settings.
entries.commentary:
Look — the simple harmonization here is plausible on its own terms and the apologists deploy it correctly. Luke 2 covers the birth and immediate postpartum, when Jesus was placed in a *phatnē* (manger/feeding trough). Matthew 2 doesn't actually narrate the birth — it picks up later, when the magi arrive. By the time the magi got to Bethlehem, the family had presumably moved into more permanent lodging — a house (*oikia*, Matt 2:11). So Luke = birth in stable/manger area, Matthew = post-birth period in a house. The two events are temporally sequential, not contradictory.

That's a reasonable surface reconciliation, and Blomberg, Carson, and the IVP commentaries all run it. The problem is that the harmonization works only if you assume both narratives are part of a single coherent timeline, which the texts don't internally support.

Here's where the harmonization frays: Matthew 2:11 says the magi found the *paidion* (young child) — not *brephos* (newborn), which is the term Luke uses in 2:12, 2:16. Matthew's word choice suggests Jesus was older than a newborn at the magi visit. Herod's subsequent order to kill all male children *up to two years old* (Matt 2:16), calculated 'according to the time he had ascertained from the magi,' suggests the magi visit occurred up to two years after the birth. So the harmonization that says 'the family just moved from stable to house in a few days' is doing more work than it acknowledges — Matthew's timeline implies the family had been in a house in Bethlehem for potentially up to two years.

Which raises the question Luke doesn't ask: why are Mary and Joseph still in Bethlehem two years after a census-trip? Luke 2:39 says they returned to Nazareth immediately after the temple presentation (40 days). Matthew's narrative requires them to still be in Bethlehem, in a house, two years later.

So the 'house vs. manger' contradiction can be papered over for the immediate birth-event, but only by exposing the much harder contradiction underneath: the two infancy narratives have incompatible geographies for the post-birth period. Luke has the family back in Nazareth within weeks. Matthew has them in a Bethlehem house long enough for Herod to chronologically calculate a two-year killing radius.

Verdict: the manger-vs-house issue is reconcilable in isolation, but reconciling it forces you into the much larger contradiction between Luke's quick-return-to-Nazareth and Matthew's protracted-Bethlehem-then-Egypt itinerary (see entry 393, 394).

entries.question: Where did Joseph and Mary live before the birth of Jesus?
entries.summary: Luke 2:1-7 says Joseph and Mary lived in Nazareth and traveled to Bethlehem only because of the census. Matthew 2:1-11 has Joseph and Mary already in Bethlehem, in a house, with no mention of a Nazareth residence or any travel. Matthew first mentions Nazareth in 2:23, after the return from Egypt — and frames the move there as fulfilling prophecy, not a homecoming.
entries.commentary:
This is the geography problem the two infancy narratives create when you read them in parallel. Luke's couple is from Nazareth (Luke 1:26 — Gabriel goes to Nazareth to find Mary). They go to Bethlehem only because of the census (Luke 2:4-5). After purification rites at the temple (Luke 2:22-38), they return home — *eis polin heautōn Nazaret* (to their own city, Nazareth — Luke 2:39).

Matthew's couple has no pre-Bethlehem backstory. The first place Joseph and Mary appear together is already in Bethlehem (Matt 2:1). They're in a house (Matt 2:11) — not a temporary census-residence, but a settled dwelling. Matthew never mentions Nazareth until the family relocates there post-Egypt as a fulfillment of prophecy (Matt 2:22-23). The Greek of 2:22-23 is interesting: *anechōrēsen eis ta merē tēs Galilaias*, then *katōkēsen eis polin legomenēn Nazaret* — 'he withdrew into the regions of Galilee... and settled in a city called Nazareth.' The verb *katōkēsen* ('settled') suggests new residence, not return.

The apologist harmonization, run by Blomberg and Witherington, tries to interleave the two. Luke covers the Nazareth → Bethlehem trip for the census. Matthew picks up later, with the family still in Bethlehem (now in a house). Luke's 'return to Nazareth' in 2:39 is then a summary that elides the Egypt detour between the temple presentation and the eventual Nazareth settlement.

That harmonization is grammatically possible but textually painful. Luke 2:39 reads (NRSV): 'When they had finished everything required by the law of the Lord, they returned to Galilee, to their own town of Nazareth.' The Greek *epestrepsan* ('they returned') plus *eis polin heautōn* ('to their own city') makes clear that Nazareth is being identified as the original home, and the chronology is presented as continuous with the temple visit — no gap for Egypt. To make this work, you have to argue Luke knew about the Egypt sojourn but suppressed it, which both Brown (*Birth of the Messiah*, pp. 224-225) and Fitzmyer (AB Luke I-IX, pp. 425-426) reject.

The simpler critical reading: Matthew and Luke had independent, incompatible traditions about where Joseph and Mary lived before the birth. Matthew assumed they were Bethlehem-natives and had to invent a reason (Herod's threat → flight to Egypt → fulfillment of 'a Nazarene shall he be called') for the family ending up in Nazareth. Luke assumed they were Nazareth-natives and had to invent a reason (the census) for the birth happening in Bethlehem. Both narratives are working to satisfy the Bethlehem-birth requirement of Micah 5:2, from opposite starting assumptions about the family's actual home.

Verdict: Luke says they lived in Nazareth before the birth. Matthew implies they lived in Bethlehem. The harmonization requires Luke to have known about Egypt and silently skipped it, which his own *epestrepsan eis polin heautōn Nazaret* refuses to support.

entries.question: Did Jesus, Mary, and Joseph go to Egypt or Nazareth?
entries.summary: Matthew 2:14 says Joseph fled with Mary and the child to Egypt 'by night' immediately after the magi left. Luke 2:39 says after the temple purification rites — about 40 days after birth, per Lev 12 — they returned directly to Nazareth. The two itineraries cannot both be true: Luke leaves no time for an Egyptian sojourn, and Matthew leaves no room for the temple presentation and Nazareth return before the flight.
entries.commentary:
This is one of the cleanest narrative contradictions in the infancy material because it's about elapsed time and itinerary, both of which are testable.

Matthew 2:13-15: angel appears to Joseph at night, immediate flight to Egypt, stay until Herod's death. Matthew 2:19-23: Herod dies (4 BCE), angel reappears, family returns from Egypt and settles in Nazareth — first time Nazareth appears in Matthew. The Egypt sojourn is dated post-magi and pre-Herod's-death.

Luke 2:21-39: circumcision on the 8th day, purification at the temple on the 40th day (Lev 12:4), then *hōs etelesan panta ta kata ton nomon kyriou, epestrepsan eis tēn Galilaian eis polin heautōn Nazaret* — 'when they had completed everything according to the law of the Lord, they returned to Galilee, to their own city Nazareth' (Luke 2:39). No Egypt. No magi. No Herodian threat. They go from the temple to Nazareth.

The two narratives place the family in two different places at roughly the same chronological moment (within the first year of Jesus's life).

The apologist harmonizations all turn on Luke 2:39 being a summary that elides the Egypt detour. Blomberg, Carson, and the IVP *Hard Sayings* crew argue Luke chose not to mention Egypt because his theological purpose was the Jerusalem-to-Galilee-to-Jerusalem trajectory, and Egypt didn't fit. Possible. But the Greek *epestrepsan* (returned) and *eis polin heautōn* (to their own city) is a continuous-action construction. There's no temporal gap signaled in the text. Luke isn't summarizing; he's narrating sequence.

More damningly, Matthew's Egypt narrative *requires* the magi visit before the flight (Matt 2:13). If you try to slot Matthew's magi-and-Egypt sequence between Luke's temple presentation (day 40) and Luke's Nazareth return (Luke 2:39), you have to assume the family went from Bethlehem → temple → back to Bethlehem → received the magi → fled to Egypt → returned from Egypt → went to Nazareth. That's three trips between Bethlehem and Jerusalem plus an Egypt detour, all silently elided by Luke's *epestrepsan*. The reconstruction is possible only in the sense that any narrative is possible if you assume the author silently omits whatever's needed.

The critical consensus (Brown, Fitzmyer, Bovon, Allison) is that the two infancy narratives are independent compositions drawing on incompatible traditions, both designed to satisfy the same theological constraints (Bethlehem birth + Nazareth upbringing) by different narrative routes. Matthew gets the family from Bethlehem to Nazareth via Egypt because his structure is Moses-typological (the Pharaoh-like Herod, the slaughter of male children, the call out of Egypt — *ex Aigyptou ekalesa ton huion mou*, Matt 2:15 quoting Hos 11:1). Luke gets them there via temple-purification because his structure is Jerusalem-centric.

Verdict: Matthew says Egypt. Luke says straight to Nazareth via the temple. The two cannot both be the actual itinerary. The harmonization that crams Egypt into the silence of Luke 2:39 is a post-hoc rationalization the Greek does not support.

entries.question: Where did John the Baptist baptize?
entries.summary: Matthew 3:6 and Mark 1:5 say John baptized people 'in the Jordan' (Greek *en tō Iordanē*); Mark 1:9 specifies that Jesus was baptized 'in the Jordan.' John 1:28 says these things happened 'in Bethany beyond the Jordan' (or 'Bethabara' in the Textus Receptus). The synoptics put the baptism in the river itself; John's gospel puts it in a settlement on the east bank.
entries.commentary:
This one is mostly a geographic gradient rather than a hard contradiction, and the harmonization works for most of it — but there's still a residual problem worth naming.

The Greek *en tō Iordanē* (Matt 3:6, Mark 1:5, 1:9) literally means 'in the Jordan,' i.e., in the river itself. The synoptic picture is of crowds standing in the water while John baptizes them. John 1:28 says the events of that day occurred *en Bēthania peran tou Iordanou* — 'in Bethany beyond the Jordan' (NA28 reads *Bēthania*; some manuscripts read *Bēthabara*, a reading promoted by Origen for theological reasons — see Metzger's *Textual Commentary*).

The surface harmonization is easy: 'Bethany beyond the Jordan' identifies a settlement near the river, and the synoptics describe the activity in the water. Both can be true — John baptized in the Jordan, near the settlement of Bethany on the east bank. Most commentators (Brown's AB John, Keener's John commentary, Köstenberger) take this route.

The residual problem is geographic specificity. The synoptics describe a generalized Judean wilderness setting near the Jordan (Mark 1:4-5). John's gospel locates the baptism at a specific east-bank settlement in Perea. The identification of this 'Bethany beyond the Jordan' is itself contested — it's not the same Bethany near Jerusalem where Lazarus lived. Origen, writing in the third century, said he couldn't find a 'Bethany' beyond the Jordan and therefore preferred the textual variant 'Bethabara.' Modern archaeology (Pixner, Murphy-O'Connor) has tentatively identified Wadi al-Kharrar / Al-Maghtas on the Jordanian side as a possible candidate, but the identification isn't certain.

The deeper critical question — flagged in Brown's AB John — is why the synoptics don't name a specific location while John specifies one, and whether the Johannine location reflects independent tradition or theological geography. The Fourth Gospel has a known interest in identifying specific sites (Aenon near Salim in John 3:23, Sychar in John 4:5), often for symbolic reasons. The fact that the synoptics and John give different specificities about the same event isn't a hard contradiction, but it does show the gospels working with different geographic source-traditions.

Verdict: this isn't a knockout contradiction. The synoptic 'in the Jordan' and the Johannine 'in Bethany beyond the Jordan' are compatible if the latter is a settlement on the river. The harmonization holds. The interesting critical question is why John bothers to specify and the synoptics don't — and what that tells you about the independence and theological geography of the Johannine source.

entries.question: Were the Pharisees baptized by John?
entries.summary: Matthew 3:7-11 says many Pharisees and Sadducees came 'to his baptism' and John spoke to them in baptismal context. Luke 7:29-30 says the Pharisees and lawyers rejected God's purpose for themselves 'not being baptized by him.' The two evangelists disagree on whether the Pharisees received John's baptism.
entries.commentary:
Matthew 3:7 — *idōn de pollous tōn Pharisaiōn kai Saddoukaiōn erchomenous epi to baptisma autou* — 'seeing many of the Pharisees and Sadducees coming to his baptism.' The phrase *erchomenous epi to baptisma autou* is the participle of *erchomai* (coming) plus *epi* (to/for) the baptism. The grammar is open — it can mean they came to be baptized, or they came to where the baptism was happening. Matthew's wording doesn't unambiguously say the Pharisees were baptized, but the context (John addresses them as supplicants and demands fruit worthy of repentance) suggests they came as potential baptizands.

Luke 7:30 — *hoi de Pharisaioi kai hoi nomikoi tēn boulēn tou theou ēthetēsan eis heautous, mē baptisthentes hyp' autou* — 'but the Pharisees and the lawyers rejected the purpose of God for themselves, not having been baptized by him.' The aorist passive participle *baptisthentes* with the negative *mē* is unambiguous: they were not baptized.

The apologist harmonization, run by Carson and Blomberg, is that Matthew describes Pharisees who *came* to the baptism site (perhaps to observe or scout John) but does not actually say they were baptized — leaving room for Luke's claim that they were not. That reading is grammatically defensible. *Erchomenous epi to baptisma autou* doesn't entail *ebaptisanto*. So Matthew = came to the scene; Luke = were not baptized. Compatible.

The weakness: Matthew's John addresses them with the same demand for repentance and fruit that he addresses to the baptized crowds — calling them *gennēmata echidnōn* (brood of vipers) and demanding *poiēsate oun karpon axion tēs metanoias* (produce fruit worthy of repentance). The pericope's whole rhetorical setup assumes they're in the queue. If Matthew thought they were just bystanders, the diatribe makes less sense — why warn potential observers to flee the wrath to come?

A stronger critical reading is that Matthew and Luke have different theological agendas with respect to John the Baptist's interactions with the Pharisees. Matthew is anti-Pharisaic and likes to depict Pharisees as failing every test, including the test of John's preaching. Luke is more interested in social-stratification — distinguishing Pharisees and lawyers (the educated elite) from 'all the people and the tax collectors' (Luke 7:29) who *did* receive John's baptism. The two evangelists are working different angles on the same general tradition that the Pharisees did not, in the end, follow John.

Verdict: the harmonization is grammatically possible but rhetorically strained. Matthew's narrative implies the Pharisees came as baptismal candidates; Luke explicitly says they weren't baptized. The two are at minimum in tension, and the harmonization papers over the redactional difference between Matthew's anti-Pharisaic frame and Luke's class-distinction frame.

entries.question: Did Jesus baptize anyone?
entries.summary: John 3:22 says Jesus and his disciples went into the land of Judea and 'there he tarried with them, and baptized' — Jesus is the explicit subject of the baptizing verb. John 4:2 then says 'though Jesus himself did not baptize, but his disciples.' The same gospel, two chapters apart, asserts opposite claims about whether Jesus performed baptisms.
entries.commentary:
This is the rare case where the contradiction is internal to a single book — John 3:22 vs. John 4:2 — and the author or a redactor seems to have noticed.

John 3:22: *ēlthen ho Iēsous kai hoi mathētai autou eis tēn Ioudaian gēn, kai ekei dietriben met' autōn kai ebaptizen* — 'Jesus came, and his disciples, into the Judean land, and there he was staying with them and was baptizing.' Singular verb *ebaptizen* (he was baptizing), with Jesus as the antecedent. The natural reading is that Jesus himself was baptizing.

John 4:2: *kaitoige Iēsous autos ouk ebaptizen all' hoi mathētai autou* — 'although Jesus himself did not baptize, but his disciples (did).' This is a direct contradiction of the most natural reading of 3:22.

The traditional harmonization — Augustine, Calvin, and reaffirmed by modern apologists like Carson and Köstenberger — is that 3:22 uses *ebaptizen* loosely to mean 'Jesus's group was baptizing,' with Jesus as the representative subject for the activity his disciples actually performed. The harmonization is grammatically conceivable (you can describe a leader as 'doing' what his subordinates do under his authority) but doesn't fit the way the rest of John 3:22-26 reads. The crowds in 3:26 explicitly identify the baptizer as the one who was with John 'beyond the Jordan' — that's clearly Jesus personally, not just his group.

The near-universal critical reading (Brown AB John, Bultmann's *The Gospel of John*, Schnackenburg's HTKNT) is that John 4:2 is a redactional gloss — an editorial parenthesis inserted at some point during the gospel's composition to correct what the redactor saw as a theological problem in 3:22. Why the correction? Because by the time the Fourth Gospel was reaching its final form, the Christian community had developed sacramental theology in which baptism is performed *into* Christ, not *by* Christ — and the idea of Jesus personally baptizing disrupted the developing sacramental framework.

The textual evidence supports the gloss-hypothesis: 4:2 is syntactically awkward, breaks the flow between 4:1 and 4:3, and uses *kaitoige* (although) — a particle that signals correction or qualification. Brown calls 4:2 a 'parenthetical remark inserted to correct a possible misimpression' (AB 29, p. 164).

Verdict: 3:22 says Jesus baptized. 4:2 says he didn't. The 'representative subject' harmonization tortures 3:22's grammar. The critical reading — that 4:2 is a later editorial gloss correcting an earlier tradition — is the parsimonious explanation. Either way, the canonical text says both things.

entries.question: How did God address Jesus at his baptism?
entries.summary: Mark 1:11 and Luke 3:22 have the heavenly voice address Jesus directly in the second person: 'You are my beloved Son' (*sy ei ho huios mou ho agapētos*). Matthew 3:17 has the voice address the crowd in the third person: 'This is my beloved Son' (*houtos estin ho huios mou ho agapētos*). The same theophany is reported with two different addressees.
entries.commentary:
This is a textbook redactional contradiction — small, well-attested, and revealing of how the gospels relate to one another.

Mark 1:11 (the earliest gospel): *sy ei ho huios mou ho agapētos, en soi eudokēsa* — 'you are my beloved Son; in you I am well pleased.' Second person direct address. The voice speaks to Jesus.

Luke 3:22 follows Mark almost verbatim: *sy ei ho huios mou ho agapētos, en soi eudokēsa* — same construction. Second person.

Matthew 3:17 changes it: *houtos estin ho huios mou ho agapētos, en hō eudokēsa* — 'this is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.' Third person. The voice speaks *about* Jesus to whoever is listening.

The apologist harmonization runs two ways. Path one: the voice said both things — 'you are my Son' to Jesus and then 'this is my Son' to the bystanders. Two separate utterances. Possible in the abstract but unsupported by any single text, and runs into the problem that all three synoptics narrate this as a single voice-event, not two.

Path two (more sophisticated): the change from *sy ei* to *houtos estin* is a translation/paraphrase issue, with one or both forms preserving the underlying Aramaic ambiguity. This is a stretch — the Greek is unambiguous in each case, and Matthew is demonstrably editing Mark, not translating an independent source.

The critical consensus (Davies-Allison, Luz, Marcus, Fitzmyer) is that Matthew has redactionally altered Mark's second-person voice to a third-person public declaration. Why? Because Matthew's baptism scene has a different theological purpose than Mark's. In Mark, the voice is a private revelation to Jesus (only Jesus 'sees the heavens torn open,' 1:10) — it's about Jesus's commissioning. In Matthew, the voice is a public proclamation to anyone present (the heavens are 'opened to him' but the announcement is broadcast) — it's about Jesus's public identification as Son.

Luke, working with both Mark and Q-or-Matthew (depending on which Synoptic theory you prefer), preserves Mark's second-person form. This pattern — Luke siding with Mark against Matthew's edits — is a recurring feature that supports Markan priority and Lukan independence from Matthew.

The contradiction is not about whether the heavens spoke. It's about whether the voice addressed Jesus or the witnesses. Mark and Luke say one thing; Matthew says another. They cannot both be verbatim accurate to a single utterance.

Verdict: Matthew has redactionally changed Mark's second-person address into a third-person declaration. The harmonization that says 'both things were said' has no textual support. The parsimonious reading is that Matthew edited his source for theological reasons.

Note on the SAB answer labels: the 'Yes'/'No' labels in the source data are malformed for this question — they don't track the actual semantic distinction (direct address vs. announcement-to-bystanders). The contradiction substance is real even though the labels are confused.

entries.question: When Jesus was tempted by the devil, what was the sequence of temptations?
entries.summary: Matthew 4:1-11 orders the temptations: (1) stones to bread, (2) pinnacle of the temple, (3) kingdoms of the world from a mountain. Luke 4:1-13 orders them: (1) stone to bread, (2) kingdoms of the world from a mountain, (3) pinnacle of the temple. The second and third temptations are swapped between the two evangelists.
entries.commentary:
This is a Q-source contradiction — both Matthew and Luke are drawing on the same hypothetical sayings source (Q), but they redactionally reorder the temptations for different theological climaxes.

Matthew 4: bread → temple → kingdoms (mountain). Matthew's climax is the mountain scene, where Satan offers Jesus *pasas tas basileias tou kosmou kai tēn doxan autōn* — 'all the kingdoms of the world and their glory.' Jesus dismisses Satan with *hypage, satana* (begone, Satan). Matthew likes mountains as theophanic loci (transfiguration mountain, Great Commission mountain), so ending the temptation cycle on the mountain fits Matthew's redactional pattern.

Luke 4: bread → kingdoms → temple. Luke's climax is the temple scene — Satan setting Jesus on the pinnacle of the temple in Jerusalem. Luke is famously Jerusalem-centric (the gospel ends in Jerusalem, Acts starts in Jerusalem), so ending the temptation in Jerusalem at the temple fits Luke's redactional geography.

The apologist harmonization, run by Carson and Blomberg, takes two main paths.

Path one: one evangelist gives the chronological order and the other gives a thematic/topical order. Possible but doesn't resolve which is which, and you can't appeal to 'topical' arrangement without conceding that at least one gospel is non-chronological in a narrative that reads chronologically.

Path two: there were actually two separate temptation cycles, and each gospel reports a different one. This is desperate even by harmonizer standards — both gospels say *forty days* of testing, both have the same three temptations with the same scripted dialogue, both end with the same departure of Satan. Two separate but identical cycles is the textbook *ad hoc* explanation.

The critical consensus (Fitzmyer, Davies-Allison, Bovon, Marshall) is that this is a clear redactional reordering of a shared Q tradition, with each evangelist arranging the temptations to climax in his preferred theological locus (mountain for Matthew, temple for Luke). The Q reconstruction is debated, but most scholars think Luke preserves the original Q order (bread → kingdoms → temple) because Luke is generally less redactional with Q material than Matthew is, and because Luke's order makes the geographical movement more dramatic (desert → high place → Jerusalem temple). Matthew has rearranged for his mountain-climax.

Verdict: Matthew and Luke disagree on temptations 2 and 3. The 'two cycles' harmonization is unparsimonious; the 'topical vs. chronological' harmonization concedes one gospel is non-chronological. The parsimonious reading is that both evangelists redacted the same Q tradition to fit their respective theological structures.

assessment.reasoning: Mainstream Synoptic scholarship (Fitzmyer, Davies-Allison, Bovon) regards the swapped second/third temptations as redactional reordering of shared Q material for differing theological climaxes; the order genuinely differs and the 'two cycles' harmonization is dismissed as ad hoc.

entries.question: Is Jesus God?
entries.summary: John 1:1, 1:14 identifies the Word (Logos) as God and says the Word became flesh — the classic textual foundation for the deity of Christ. James 1:13 says God cannot be tempted with evil. Hebrews 4:15 (and the temptation narratives in Matthew 4, Luke 4) says Jesus was tempted in every way. If Jesus is God and God cannot be tempted, but Jesus was tempted, the syllogism collapses.
entries.commentary:
This is a syllogistic contradiction built from three premises rather than two opposing verses, which is why it requires walking through carefully.

Premise 1 (John 1:1, 1:14): *en archē ēn ho logos, kai ho logos ēn pros ton theon, kai theos ēn ho logos*. The Word was God. The Word became flesh and dwelt among us. The Johannine prologue is the canonical foundation for Logos Christology and, alongside passages like Col 1:15-20 and Heb 1:3, the textual basis for Nicene Trinitarianism.

Premise 2 (James 1:13): God cannot be tempted with evil (*apeirastos kakōn*). See entry 384.

Premise 3 (Heb 4:15; Matt 4:1; Luke 4:1-2): Jesus was tempted in every respect (*pepeirasmenon de kata panta kath' homoiotēta*, Heb 4:15).

Logical inference: if Jesus = God (premise 1), and God cannot be tempted (premise 2), then Jesus cannot be tempted. But Jesus was tempted (premise 3). Contradiction.

The Christological harmonization developed in the patristic period and codified at Chalcedon (451 CE) is that Jesus has two natures — divine and human — and was tempted *kata sarka* (according to the flesh, in his human nature) while remaining untemptable *kata pneuma* (according to the spirit, in his divine nature). The Communicatio Idiomatum doctrine — predications proper to one nature can be ascribed to the person — allows orthodox Christians to say 'Jesus was tempted' (true of his human nature) and 'God cannot be tempted' (true of his divine nature) without formal contradiction.

This is a theological move, not a textual one. The biblical authors themselves do not parse this in two-natures terms. James 1:13 is categorical: *ho theos apeirastos estin kakōn* — God is untemptable. Hebrews 4:15 is categorical: Jesus was tempted *kata panta* (in every respect). The biblical writers don't carve out a 'tempted-only-in-his-human-nature' exception. The two-natures distinction is patristic-era systematic theology back-applied to the texts.

Bart Ehrman's *How Jesus Became God* (HarperOne, 2014) is the canonical popular-level treatment of how the deity-of-Christ claim developed historically through stages — from low Christology (Jesus as exalted human messiah, early Pauline material) to high Christology (Jesus as pre-existent divine Word, Johannine prologue) — and how the resulting tensions with the canonical statements about God's nature (immutable, impassible, untemptable) required centuries of theological work to systematize. The systematizing took ecumenical councils and doctrinal language (homoousios, hypostatic union) precisely because the raw textual data does produce tensions like the one this contradiction names.

The non-Trinitarian harmonization — used by Unitarians, Jehovah's Witnesses, and various early-church Adoptionists — simply denies premise 1: Jesus was not God, the Johannine Logos language is metaphorical, and there's no syllogistic problem. That's a coherent position textually but a heterodox one.

Verdict: orthodox Trinitarianism resolves the contradiction by invoking the two-natures doctrine, which works as systematic theology but isn't textually grounded in James or Hebrews themselves. The texts as written produce the contradiction the SAB names. The harmonization requires Chalcedonian Christology to be read into texts that predate it by 350+ years. Take your pick: textually consistent and non-Trinitarian, or Trinitarian and post-Chalcedonian-systematic.
